## What does freeze-dried instant coffee mean for an Indian kitchen?

Freeze-drying skips the liquid stage entirely. Frozen coffee concentrate goes straight from solid to vapor under vacuum, so the aromatic oils that usually disappear in high-heat spray drying stay locked inside the granule. The result is a lighter, porous crystal that rehydrates instantly and tastes much closer to a freshly pulled shot. In an Indian kitchen where the geyser hisses and mornings move fast, that speed matters — you get cafe-quality depth without the wait. A practical tip: use water just off the boil, around 92–94°C, and stir gently; the granules bloom in seconds and you avoid the scorched note that rolling-boil water can leave. Purity Beans applies this method to its Purica and Purista jars, while the Bold jar uses agglomeration for a denser granule that holds up in milk-heavy cups. Ultra Blend sits at 70% coffee and 30% chicory for drinkers who want a familiar, everyday balance, and Prima is a pure Arabica agglomerate that is not freeze-dried. Pick the process that matches how you actually brew.

### A plain definition

Whatever brought you here, the label settles it. The other single jars on this page are 0% chicory.

## How do you read the chicory line on the jar?

Turn the jar around and find the ingredient list. That is the only line that matters. If it says chicory, the blend contains chicory — no marketing phrase on the front can change that. At Purity Beans, Bold, Purista, and Purica all show coffee as the single ingredient because they are pure coffee with zero chicory. Purista and Purica are freeze-dried granules; Bold is agglomerated pure coffee. A quick rule of thumb: the higher chicory sits on the list, the more of it you are drinking. Some brands tuck it near the bottom and hope you won't check. Prima is pure Arabica but it is agglomerated, not freeze-dried, so the process line will read differently. Next time you pick up a jar, ignore the flavor adjectives and read the ingredients. That five-second habit tells you more than any advertisement ever will.

## Which jar suits the way you drink coffee?

Choosing a jar comes down to how you actually drink your coffee. If you reach for a mug of black coffee first thing in the morning and want that deep, honest kick, Bold is the one — it's agglomerated, strong, and priced at ₹369 for 100g. For afternoons when you want something smooth with natural crema, Purista brings freeze-dried Robusta at ₹509 for 100g. And if your ideal cup leans aromatic with caramel and chocolate notes, Purica delivers freeze-dried Arabica at ₹559 for 100g. Not sure where you land? The Variety Box (₹877 for four 50g jars) lets you taste all four side by side. Purity Beans keeps it simple: match the jar to the ritual, and you will never waste money on coffee that does not fit your morning.

## What does each jar cost in rupees?

If you are budgeting for a shelf of Purity Beans jars, here is how the prices break down today. ## How do people brew instant coffee in Indian cities?

In most Indian city kitchens, the ritual is simple: water hits a rolling boil, a spoonful of granules goes into the mug, then milk and sugar follow. Some people swear by dissolving the coffee in a tiny splash of hot water first — a quick stir until it turns glossy — before topping up with steaming milk. That extra ten seconds stops the granules from clumping at the bottom. Others skip the fuss entirely and dump everything into the saucepan, letting it bubble once before pouring. Office pantries see the electric kettle method: hot water straight into the cup, a dash of cold milk to temper it, done in thirty seconds. On slower Sunday mornings, you'll find the whisk come out — vigorous back-and-forth until a thin caramel foam crowns the surface, the closest thing to cafe texture without a machine. Walking down the coffee aisle can feel a bit overwhelming with all the loud claims staring back from every shelf. Take a quiet minute to check what is actually inside your pantry staples.
